# Education in New Zealand
Education in New Zealand is characterized by a free, compulsory, and secular schooling system for residents aged 5 to 19, with mandatory attendance between 6 and 16 years old. The system is structured into 13 year levels, with primary education (Years 1–8), secondary education (Years 9–13), and special schools and alternatives like home-schooling and Māori-medium education. Early childhood education, which is not government-owned but licensed, is widely attended through kindergartens, kōhanga reo, playcentres, and other services. State schools are government-funded and free, while state-integrated schools and private schools charge various fees. The national curriculum outlines key learning areas and is followed by most schools, culminating in senior students typically working toward the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA), with some schools also offering alternative qualifications.
Provision for Māori-language education has increased in recent decades, featuring options such as immersion schools (kura kaupapa Māori) and mainstream schools offering Māori as a subject. Funding for schools is determined on a per-student basis, with adjustments for school size and socio-economic decile, while tertiary education funding combines government subsidies and student fees. Educational challenges include declining math and science achievement in international rankings, ongoing efforts to address school bullying, and disparities in outcomes for Māori and Pacific Island students. The system also features enrolment zones in urban areas to manage school capacity, offers various types of schools by years and function, and has a history of adapting to practical and academic educational demands.
